summary: On Linux with an NVIDIA card the window no longer flashes empty.
changes: With WebKitGTK 2.54 and NVIDIA's driver, the window flashed empty several times a second while a project was working: for a frame only what had just changed was drawn — the tab's pulsing dot, the terminal cursor, the scrollbar — and the desktop showed through the rest. A part nothing redrew could stay blank. It came from the way Beacon had to draw on NVIDIA until now, without DMA-BUF, which WebKitGTK 2.54 no longer does correctly; on 2.54 Beacon draws through DMA-BUF again, and every frame arrives whole.

On an older WebKitGTK nothing changes. If your machine still closes the window on start with WebKitGTK 2.54, setting WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 brings the old way back, and Beacon leaves that choice alone.

summary: Switching account works: 0.10.0 killed the session instead of opening it.
changes: Switching Claude Code to another account and coming back to the project ended the session before it drew anything — "No conversation found with session ID" — and left no way to sign in to the new account, because the sign-in screen is what that session would have shown. The conversation was real, in the account just left: it lives inside that account's folder, so it belongs to one account and cannot be opened from another. Beacon asks to continue a conversation only in the account it was had in, and starts a new one otherwise.

The conversations offered in the menu are the ones the account in use can actually open. Asking to resume one from another account says so, and says to switch back to it, rather than leaving the session to die on the agent's own error.
The context percentage showed the other account's and never moved. It belongs to a conversation, and the conversation was the one Beacon should no longer have been in. It follows the account now.
A message in the status bar is only red when something is wrong. "Claude Code will use Work from its next start" — a switch that had just worked — arrived in the colour a crash arrives in.

The session daemon keeps the log of the previous run beside the current one. Updating Beacon and then restarting it used to write over the only account of whatever went wrong, which is the run anybody would be asking about.

summary: Each agent can be signed in to more than one account, and its panel says which one it is using.
changes: Each agent's panel header names the account it is signed in to. Claude Code is asked for it — the email and the plan — so what is on screen is what Claude Code itself reports. Codex has no way to say which account it is on, only how it signed in, so it shows that and the name you gave the account.

That name opens a menu, and one click changes which account the agent uses. An account is a folder the agent keeps its own settings, history and sign-in in — Beacon points the agent at it with the variable the agent documents for exactly this, and nothing else. No credential of yours is read, written, copied or moved, and there is no sign-in screen in Beacon: Add an account makes an empty folder, and you sign in by running the agent's own login in the project's terminal, where it will already be pointed at the new account.

Switching applies the next time that agent starts, which the menu says rather than leaving you to notice. A running agent keeps the account it was started with — that is what an environment variable is — and the conversation does not come along either, because it stays with the account it happened in. The panel's Restart button is in the same header.

Whatever Beacon has been allowed to install into an agent's configuration goes into every account, and a new account inherits it. Without that, an account you switched to would have no hooks: no amber tab, no "waiting for you", and no resuming a conversation. Forgetting an account leaves its folder alone — it holds your settings and a live credential, and forgetting is reversible where deleting is not.

Check again in Settings → Requirements used to update only that screen. Installing Claude Code, pressing it and going back left the panel still showing the install instructions. It tells the whole window now.

This update replaces the session daemon once, so anything running when you install it ends. The daemon has to be the one that understands which account to start a session with; an older one would ignore it and start your work on the wrong subscription without anything saying so.

summary: Variables can be added to a .env and changed from its view, and the editor panel has one close button.
changes: The .env view adds variables. Add variable opens a row for a name and a value; typing = in the name moves on to the value, pasting a KEY=value line fills in both, and pasting several lists them so they can be added at once. Each row has Edit, which changes the value where it stands and keeps an export or a comment at the end of the line. Edit as text opens the whole file in the editor, with a way back to the variables.

What the view writes is read back exactly as it was typed: quoted where it has to be, a private key keeping its line breaks, and a value that cannot be written faithfully refused rather than changed. It saves the way the editor does, so a file Claude changed in the meantime is not written over.
A .env saved by a Windows editor showed every variable but its first, and a comment after a quoted value — A="x" # note — made the quotes part of the value. Both read correctly now.
The editor panel's header showed two close buttons. It shows one. Contributed by jimy-k4.

summary: Beacon opens on Linux with an NVIDIA card, types accents in the terminal, draws your terminal font's icons, and can be installed on Arch as a package.
changes: On Linux with NVIDIA's driver, Beacon opened a transparent window that never filled in and then quit. WebKitGTK's DMA-BUF renderer was having the connection to the compositor closed on its first frame. Beacon now turns that renderer off before the window starts when the driver is loaded, unless you have set WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER yourself.

Accents typed in a Linux terminal arrive once. A dead key — ´ then a, as a Spanish layout types every accent — used to bring older characters with it, so pingüino arrived as pingó ñ üino. Input methods that compose Japanese, Chinese or Korean are left exactly as they were.

The terminal's font is yours to choose, in Settings → Terminal: a family and a size, applied as you change them. On Linux it suggests the monospace fonts you have installed. With nothing chosen, Beacon now tries the common Nerd Fonts first, so a Powerlevel10k or starship prompt draws its icons instead of boxes.

Beacon can be installed on Arch Linux as a package, beacon-split-bin, which runs on Arch's own WebKitGTK and natively on Wayland. The release now carries a .deb, which is what that package is made from. Installed by a package manager, Beacon leaves updating to it rather than offering an update it cannot install.

summary: Click an image in the files panel and you see it, and anything Beacon will not show opens in whatever this machine opens it with.
changes: Clicking an image in the files panel shows it. It used to say "logo.png is not a text file", which is true and useless. What counts as an image is read from the file's own first bytes rather than from its name, so a .png that is not one is described instead of drawn as a broken picture, and a screenshot saved without an extension is shown anyway. PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, ICO and WebP. An SVG still opens as text, which is the form you are most likely to want to change.
An image says its dimensions beside its size, which is usually the reason an asset gets opened at all.

A picture no longer has to fit the editor's limit. That limit is about what is sensible to put in a text editor, and a screenshot of a large display is routinely past it — "too large to edit here" about a picture you were never going to edit reads as something broken. Images go to sixteen megabytes.

Anything Beacon will not show — a PDF, a video, an archive, a picture past even that — offers to open with whatever this machine opens it with. Beacon does not carry viewers of its own: a PDF drawn in the window would work on macOS and Windows and not on Linux, and your machine already has something that opens all of them properly.

summary: Beacon runs on Linux, and it can be told to look at your machine again instead of insisting something is missing after you have installed it.
changes: Beacon runs on Linux, as an AppImage. The window draws its own controls, the install commands it offers are the ones your distribution uses, and the session daemon is kept outside the image — an AppImage is mounted somewhere different on every launch, so a daemon named from inside it would be named somewhere that no longer exists by the next time you opened Beacon, and the hooks that tell a tab what its agent is doing would quietly stop working.

"Check again" in Requirements checks again. It did not: everything Beacon had worked out about your machine — where each program was, what your login shell's PATH is, what each agent can do — was worked out once and kept for as long as Beacon ran. So the common way to meet Beacon was to be told Claude Code was missing, install it, come back, and be told the same thing, with a restart as the only way out and nothing to say so.

A requirement has four answers now rather than two: ready, missing, not answering, or waiting to be signed in. Only the missing one is offered an install command — being told to install something you are looking at is how a program convinces you it is not listening. Whether you are signed in is asked of the agent itself, by the same question you could type; Beacon never touches a credential.

An install command can be put straight into a terminal here, on its command line, with the keyboard in it. It stops short of pressing Return: running an installer is a decision, and the command is readable and one key away.
The first-run guide ends on what Beacon actually found — ready, needing a sign-in, missing, or not answering — rather than telling everybody to sign in to something that might not be there.

The allowance and the context in the status bar grey out separately, so a figure from two hours ago no longer looks as current as one from ten seconds ago. After the session daemon restarts, an allowance whose age Beacon cannot vouch for says so instead of claiming it was just reported. Contributed by jimy-k4.

summary: The status bar says what Codex is spending, the git panel follows the agent you are working in, and the files panel searches a project of any size without quietly missing half of it.
changes: The status bar says what Codex is spending, not only Claude. Codex has no status line to ask, but it writes the numbers down: every turn it records how much of the context window the conversation is using and how much of both its rate-limit windows is gone. Beacon reads them. The two allowances are kept apart — Claude's is Anthropic's and Codex's is OpenAI's — and the meter follows the agent you are working in, naming it whenever there is another agent it could have been.

The git panel reads the checkout of the agent you are working in. With a checkout each, reading Claude's diff while working in Codex is how somebody commits the wrong thing, and nothing in the files themselves says which one you are in. Pressing the control still looks anywhere, and going back to an agent panel puts it in step again. The control also looks like a control now, and its label no longer breaks across two lines in a narrow panel.

The files panel's search works in a project of any size, and says when it had to stop. The listing is capped, and where the search would have said "no matches" it now says how many files it looked at — so a file it never read is not reported as a file that does not exist. The listing also runs off the thread that answers the window, so a large repository no longer makes the first keystroke of a search wait. Contributed by jimy-k4.

The first-run guide is seven steps instead of twelve. A panel you have put away no longer gets a step of its own, and files, editor, terminal and git share one. The keyboard step says which panels are hidden and that the palette brings them back.
Ctrl/⌘+G's go-to-line panel is the app's rather than CodeMirror's grey buttons, and opening a file from the search brings its row into view in the tree. Contributed by jimy-k4.

The five-hour allowance is ordered by its own numbers before its dates: a later reset time wins outright, and within one window the higher percentage does. A daemon that has just restarted can no longer let an idle session's old figure outrank a session that has just replied. The allowance and the context are dated apart, so one being old no longer dims the other. Contributed by jimy-k4.
Reopening a conversation works from Claude Code's own transcript, with a test to keep it working. Contributed by jimy-k4.

Codex can be restarted from a project's menu, where only Claude and the terminal could be. The checkout setting in that menu is one line again instead of a paragraph, and Settings says what Codex reports rather than pointing at Claude's page.

Beacon no longer takes a Claude Code parent's switches as your own. Started from a Claude Code tool — which is how Beacon is usually developed — it passed `NO_COLOR` and `GIT_EDITOR` to every session, so Claude drew itself without colour and `git commit` aborted on an empty message without opening an editor. Switches somebody may have set in their own shell profile are left alone. Contributed by jimy-k4.

summary: A guide on your first run, one sign-in for every project, a chime when Claude needs you, search in the files panel, and the settings grouped by what they are about.
changes: A short guide on the first run says what is where, and offers the basics — theme, notifications and the two sounds — before you have to go looking for them. Seven steps on a new install, and the last one is the Claude panel, where signing in happens. Escape skips it, it never comes back uninvited, and “Show the welcome guide” in the command palette brings it back. Contributed by jimy-k4.
Sign in to Claude Code once and every open project picks it up, instead of each one asking in turn. Contributed by jimy-k4.

Beacon chimes when Claude has finished or needs an answer, and the last reply stays above the terminal until the next turn starts, so you can read it without scrolling back. Both sounds start off. Contributed by jimy-k4.

The files panel has a search field. Typing lists the matching files with the matched letters marked, ↑ and ↓ walk them and Return opens one, which also reveals it in the tree. The list is read fresh each time, so a file an agent has just written is found. Contributed by jimy-k4.
Settings are grouped by what they are about rather than listed in one column.

The terminal is legible in the light theme. The sixteen colours a program can ask for were xterm's, made for a dark background, so a program's white came out white on near-white — Claude Code's questions worst of all. There is a light palette now, every colour clears the contrast floor against the window, and any colour a program picks for itself is lifted to meet it. Contributed by jimy-k4.

The five-hour allowance in the status bar is dated by when the number was new rather than by when Beacon heard it. A session repeating itself, or reopening the window, no longer makes the morning's figure look current, and an idle project can no longer overwrite what a working one reported. Past the reset time it says so instead of showing the old window's percentage. Contributed by jimy-k4.
The editor's find panel is the app's, rather than CodeMirror's grey buttons and grey border. Contributed by jimy-k4.
A development build no longer looks for updates. Contributed by jimy-k4.

summary: Shift+Enter breaks the line, @ and # can be typed on any keyboard, and updating on Windows no longer leaves the old daemon behind.
changes: Shift+Enter starts a new line in the Claude and Codex panels instead of sending a prompt you had not finished. A terminal cannot tell it from Enter, so Beacon now sends each agent the newline it actually reads. A shell is left alone, where Enter running the command is the point — and so is an input method in the middle of composing.

@, #, brackets and braces can be typed again on Spanish and most other non-US Mac keyboards. They live on the Option key there, and the terminal was treating Option as Meta, so each one arrived as an escape sequence and nothing appeared. Option with an arrow, Backspace or Enter still does what it did.

Updating on Windows no longer leaves the old session daemon in place. A running program cannot be overwritten there, and the daemon nearly always is running, so the 0.6.0 update could leave a 0.5 daemon beside a 0.6 window and end in "could not reach the session daemon". The installer now moves it aside so the new one can take its place; and if an old daemon is ever found again, Beacon says so and what fixes it. Contributed by jimy-k4.

Without Beacon's hooks installed, reopening a conversation works. Beacon only learned that Claude Code had saved a conversation from the hooks, so without them every start after the first asked for it as new and Claude Code refused with "Session ID … is already in use". Beacon now looks for the conversation on disk. Contributed by jimy-k4.

The dimmer text in the dark theme can be read in daylight. The quietest two levels — panel headers, the status bar, placeholders — were well below what body text needs once the screen catches some sun; all four levels are now brighter and evenly spaced, so the order between them stays. Contributed by jimy-k4.

summary: Beacon runs on Windows, and Codex runs beside Claude Code — in its own panel, its own conversation, and if you want it, its own checkout.
changes: Beacon runs on Windows 10 and 11. The whole of it: the session daemon, real terminals, the clip drawer, the hooks that tell a tab what Claude is doing. The window draws its own caption buttons and the installer comes as both an NSIS setup and an MSI. Contributed by jimy-k4, built and used on a real Windows machine, and now checked on every push alongside macOS.

Codex is a second agent, not a replacement. It gets a panel of its own (⌘⇧O), its own conversations, and can run at the same time as Claude Code in the same project. It starts hidden, so nothing moves until you ask for it. Settings → Codex installs the small plugin that lets it report what it is doing; Codex will not run a hook it has not been shown, so there is one step left to you afterwards, and that screen says so.

Every session can reach the programs you installed. Started from the Dock, Beacon had nothing on its PATH but the four system directories, and an agent inherits that — so `node`, `cargo`, anything a version manager put there, and any hook that needed them, were simply not found. Sessions now run with the PATH your login shell sets. A terminal panel never showed this, because a shell works its own out.

A project can give each agent a checkout of its own. Two agents editing the same files means the second one to save wins; turning this on puts each in a git worktree instead, on its own branch, and leaves the project directory to you. Off unless you ask for it. The git panel can be pointed at any of them to read what an agent has done — the file tree and the editor always stay on your own copy, so saving always writes where you think it does.
When the session daemon will not start, it says why. It had been explaining itself perfectly well to a stream pointed at nowhere, while every panel showed the one thing you could already see.
An agent installed with npm starts. Those are not binaries but scripts that need their interpreter, and Beacon found them and could not run them — which looks exactly like not having installed them.

The file tree says what each thing is before saying what it is called. A hundred or so endings and the names you know at a glance — package.json is not merely some JSON, and package-lock.json is not merely some package.json. Anything unrecognised gets a plain file, never a blank.

Reopening no longer shows a panel of shredded text. A terminal was being built at eighty columns and then filled with output that had been wrapped for a different width; it is now built at the width that output was written for. Pressing Resume used to be the way out of it.

summary: Resume works on a conversation you have not spoken in yet, the splitters move again, and files appear the moment something makes them.
changes: Resume no longer answers "No conversation found with session ID". Beacon treated starting a Claude as proof that a conversation existed, but Claude Code writes nothing until the first exchange — so a session you opened and never typed into left nothing to go back to, and asking to resume it replaced the panel with an error. Whether a conversation exists is now decided by something having been said in it.

A fork you have not typed in yet keeps the history it was forked from. Looking at another conversation and coming back — or a daemon that had been replaced in between — used to start it as an empty conversation wearing the same name, with the history it was forked from silently gone.

A missing MCP configuration no longer costs you the whole panel. Beacon writes that file once, into the temporary directory macOS sweeps every few days; when it was swept, Claude Code was handed a path to nothing and refused to start at all. It is written again when it is missing, and if it cannot be, the session starts without the clip drawer and says so rather than failing.

The splitters work again once a panel is hidden. Hiding one changes the shape of the layout, and the splitters were still reporting where they used to be — so a drag resized a split that was not on screen and the panels sat there, unmovable, however hard you pulled.

Files appear in the tree as they are made. The tree re-read when the window regained focus, which never happens when the thing writing the files is the Claude in the panel beside it, so a new file stayed invisible until you clicked away and back or pressed refresh.

summary: Updating no longer greets you with a window that thinks it is offline.
changes: The first launch after an update stopped saying the daemon went away. An update that moves the protocol finds the previous version's daemon still running and has to swap it, which is expected — but the swap was announced as a failure, and every panel in a window that had not finished opening said so. Nothing took it back, because the notice that clears it only follows a real reconnection.

A connection that has been replaced can no longer take its replacement with it. A reader notices its stream ended some time after it did, by which point another connection may already be in place; it used to pull that one down too, and one planned swap became a window that stayed offline until it was restarted.
Beacon no longer starts two daemons at once. The window opening and the reconnect loop could each start one, which left it attached twice and hearing every event two times.

Not finding the claude command is no longer remembered. Where Claude Code lives comes from your login shell, which is given four seconds to answer and can miss that on a machine that is briefly busy — right after an update, say. The daemon outlives the window, so one missed answer used to mean every session for the rest of the day was told Claude Code was not installed.

summary: A project holds several named Claude conversations, and you can tell which one you are in.
changes: Claude sessions have names and come back. A project is no longer one nameless conversation that grows until most of it is work nobody is doing any more: start a workstream for the thing you are about to do, name it, and come back to it later from the chip in the panel header. Beacon gives each conversation its id when it starts it, so this needs a recent Claude Code — where the flags are missing, the chip is not there and nothing else changes.

Restarting Claude no longer throws the conversation away. The header button says Resume, and it does: the process starts again and carries on where it was. Starting clean is a deliberate act now, with a name attached.

Beacon refuses to open one conversation in two Claudes. It asks Claude Code what is running rather than assuming, and offers to fork instead — which keeps the history and leaves the original where it is.

The usage panel says more, because Claude Code does. How full the context is, in bands rather than a bare number; whether the prompt cache is warm, and what a cold one would cost to rebuild; the model, the effort, the week and the five-hour window. When Claude Code says nothing about something, Beacon says nothing about it either.

One piece of advice at a time, and never acted on. A large context whose cache has gone cold is worth knowing about at the moment it starts costing something. What to do about it is yours: Beacon does not compact, does not clear, and does not start a session on your behalf.

Three small agents, offered to the sessions Beacon starts. One searches the repository, one runs tests, one reviews a finished change with fresh eyes — each there to keep a large pile of output out of the conversation doing the work. They are handed to Claude Code per session, so nothing is written into your projects and the agents you already have are untouched. There is a switch in Settings, because their descriptions cost context whether they are used or not.
The header says when work has been delegated. From outside, a session that has handed a large search to a subagent looks exactly like one that has gone quiet.

Git handles a conflicted file as one. It is shown separately, kept out of stage and unstage — which used to mark it resolved with its markers still in place — and staging everything refuses to sweep it up. A commit is blocked while conflicts are unresolved, and says so. Every git command now has a deadline, so nothing git waits for can take the panel with it.

Saving is atomic and refuses to overwrite a file that moved underneath it, which in this application usually means Claude. A clean buffer reloads; a dirty one asks, because one choice loses your typing and the other loses Claude's.

Quitting with unsaved work asks first. The file tree can show dotfiles, and can move a file somewhere else. Notifications go through macOS directly, so they arrive when Beacon is not the application in front.
The hooks need installing again for this: open Settings and reinstall them. Beacon now listens for subagents starting and finishing, which is two events it did not register before.

summary: Claude can hand you something worth keeping, and it survives the trip to the clipboard.
changes: Claude can file a clip from inside a session — a command, an address, the body of an email — and it lands in a drawer beside the session with a copy button. Beacon gives each session a small tool of its own for this, so nothing has to be hunted out of a scrolling transcript and selected by hand.
The drawer keeps a clip book per project: it survives closing Beacon, and one button clears the lot when a clip has served its purpose.

Accents and dashes reach the clipboard intact. Started from the Dock, Beacon inherited no locale at all, and `pbcopy` reads a missing locale as Mac OS Roman — so an em dash copied from inside a session arrived as `‚Äî`. Sessions are given a UTF-8 locale now when nothing else has set one.

summary: A tab knows Claude is there before you have said anything to it.
changes: Beacon hears about a Claude session when it starts, not when you send it its first message. Until now the first hook of a session was the one that submits a prompt, so a tab you had just opened said nothing about the Claude sitting in it.

Resuming or clearing a session takes back what the tab was still claiming. "Waiting for you" and "finished" are never expired on a timer — both can honestly last hours — so a session left at a permission prompt and then resumed used to ask for an answer nobody owed it any more.
The hooks need installing again for this: open Settings and reinstall them, or Beacon will show them as stale until you do.

summary: The hooks actually run, and the panel holding your keyboard says so.
changes: Claude Code's hooks work from an installed copy. The application lives at `/Applications/Beacon Split.app`, and the space in that path meant the shell Claude runs hooks through read the command as ending at `/Applications/Beacon`, so every hook failed.

Installing the hooks twice no longer leaves two of them behind. Beacon looked for its own entries by product name, which appears in a development checkout's path and never in an installed build's, so each install added a copy rather than replacing one. Reinstalling from this version clears the duplicates.

Beacon finds the `claude` binary when it was started from the Dock. It asked an interactive shell where the binary lived, which a prompt theme or a git status daemon can wedge forever; the probe now gives up after four seconds and falls back to where the installers actually write.
The panel your keyboard is in is edged in the workspace colour, and ⌥⌘← / ⌥⌘→ move between panels.
The session panel no longer draws a slab of accent colour over its own contents.
A new application icon.

summary: The first build worth handing to somebody else.
changes: Workspaces group projects, each with its own colour and icon, so you know where you are before reading anything.
A real claude session and a real shell per project, in their own PTYs. Beacon runs the CLI you already use rather than reimplementing it.
Sessions outlive the window: close Beacon and they keep running, open it again and it reattaches to them.
Layouts are a tree of splits with four presets, and every divider is draggable.
A file tree with an editor, a .env view that keeps values hidden until asked, and git status, diff, stage and commit.
Command palette on ⌘K, quick open on ⌘P, and every shortcut is editable.
Tabs say what Claude is doing — working, finished, or waiting for you — reported by Claude Code rather than guessed from output.
The title bar shows how much of the five-hour allowance is left and how full each project's context is.
Light and dark themes, how much of the desktop shows through the window, and whether what shows through is frosted.
